anomaly_def.Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write bandwidth or IOPS on the underlying storage devices is saturated, driving up I/O latency and queue depths independent of database engine settings.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cycles are exhausted, leaving insufficient compute capacity for database foreground and background tasks, which inflates run-queue waits and overall response time.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, processes/threads, shared memory, AIO contexts, or other kernel objects are reached, preventing the database from allocating required OS resources.

When these three root causes arise concurrently, the database exhibits a multi-layer resource crunch: 1) response times degrade as I/O queues lengthen and disk latencies spike, 2) CPU utilization plateaus at or near 100 %, with elevated context-switch and scheduler waits, while some processes spin or back-off waiting for I/O, and 3) new sessions, background workers, or asynchronous I/O requests intermittently fail with OS-level "resource exhausted" errors. Wait-event profiles simultaneously show heavy data-file/log-file I/O waits, CPU run-queue waits, and sudden surges in OS-error-related waits. Batch windows overrun, interactive transactions stall, and recovery or checkpoint operations lag, making it difficult to pinpoint a single bottleneck because symptoms oscillate between compute, I/O, and kernel allocation failures.

Causally, the three anomalies can reinforce one another in a vicious cycle: storage saturation elongates I/O service times, causing worker threads to hold CPU longer or spin in kernel space, which raises overall CPU demand. Elevated CPU load inflates context switching and system-call overhead, consuming additional kernel objects (threads, AIO contexts) and pushing the process toward OS resource limits. Once those limits are reached, failed allocations further stall I/O submission and worker scheduling, deepening both the storage backlog and CPU queuing. Conversely, hitting OS limits (e.g., AIO context caps or file-descriptor ceilings) can throttle parallel I/O issuance, reducing effective throughput while worker threads busy-wait, inflating CPU usage. The intertwined feedback loops between saturated disks, maxed-out CPUs, and exhausted kernel limits rapidly deteriorate database throughput and availability unless all three layers are relieved together.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
